newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Cr Lyonnais finds bright spot in Asia.
newsitem.headline: Cr Lyonnais finds bright spot in Asia.

text.p: Asia, along with the U.S. and Eastern Europe, is expected to remain one of the bright spots for ailing French bank Credit Lyonnais' global business, bank chairman Jean Peyrelevade said Monday.
Outside of its troubled commercial banking business in Europe, Credit Lyonnais is performing well and in line with international standards, he said.

"If I consider American, Asian and Eastern European operations, plus our capital markets activities, our return on equity is slightly below 20 percent, which is approximately that of American or British banks," he said.
Peyrelevade said that 1996 will be the best year for the bank's Asian operations, which should show net profit after taxes of "not far from US$150 million."

He said that the bank realises a higher return on equity in Eastern Europe than in Asia, while the return on equity is higher in Asia than in the U.S. But the bank makes more money in the U.S. than in Asia because its operations are bigger there, he said.

The bank's Asian business is split more or less evenly between commercial and investment banking. In 1996, Asian business grew at a rate of 30 percent versus 1995 and Peyrelevade said a growth rate of 20 percent going into 1997 "would be quite satisfactory."
Credit Lyonnais, which already has been bailed out twice by the French government, expects to receive a third bailout in order to make the bank ready for privatization.
Peyrelevade reiterated that he does not expect the bank to be ready for sale for about two years.
He said the bank is expected to break even this year, but it still needs to improve profitability.
"We should divest to some extent in retail banking in Europe," he said, while declining to name specific assets.

The chairman said Credit Lyonnais does not intend to sell major assets in the U.S., Asia or Eastern Europe as yet. He added that any modest divestitures of assets in these areas would reflect stategic decisions and not a change in business focus.
Peyrelevade also said that the bank has no plan to give up any of its asset management business.
"On the contrary, we plan to develop it because it is a business that does not need a high level of equity and we have all the necessary expertise," he said.
Peyrelevade said the European banking sector is "difficult" and should remain that way for the next two to five years.
The advent of a single European currency in 1999 will have an immediate depressing effect on Europe's banking sector as foreign exchange business diminishes, he noted.
But in the longer term, the Euro should spur more foreign investment in Europe because the single currency will create better liquidity in financial markets, he said.
